article.opening: After moving through {{priorSign}} from {{priorSignEntryDate}} to {{priorSignExitDate}}, Mars enters Aquarius on {{entryDate}}, and the old method suddenly becomes harder to tolerate. The usual workaround looks wasteful. A group tests the odd idea that had been dismissed. Someone else cuts a repeated step that no longer helps. Mars in Aquarius moves quickly when a familiar setup no longer fits what comes next.
article.tension: That speed has a cost. Once the new approach works, every objection can look like proof that someone is stuck in the past. We stop explaining, make the change without the person affected by it, and treat resistance as evidence that the old way is broken. The idea may be better. Digging in still turns a useful disruption into another fight, and the group stops trusting how decisions get made.
article.development: Mars last moved through Aquarius from {{previousResidencyEntryDate}} to {{previousResidencyExitDate}}. The same pressure returns wherever an outdated pattern is wasting energy. We may replace a clumsy tool, abandon a rule that no longer serves its purpose, or name what a group has avoided because agreement mattered more than accuracy. Then the focus narrows. The person in front of us becomes part of the obstacle, and independence hardens into refusal. A change made in the name of the future can reproduce the same problem it meant to end: one fixed answer, imposed by whoever moved first.
article.close: Before {{exitDate}}, we may replace the stale pattern and lose the trust needed for the new one to work.
try_this: We can skip one repeated step that no longer helps and note whether anything actually suffers this week.
We can ask one person affected by a recent change what became harder after it.
We can spend an hour testing an unfamiliar tool on a small recurring problem.
